title: Love those who stumble
hookLine: love even those who do wrong; they're kin and err unwillingly (Meditations 7.22)

cards: A toddler learning to walk falls over. Nobody gets angry at the toddler. Nobody says, he's doing that to me.
You see a small person who hasn't learned yet, and you reach out a hand. Now picture an adult who lies to you, or snaps at you, or lets you down. The reaching hand disappears.
Marcus Aurelius wondered whether the two cases are as different as they feel, and in book seven he says something that sounds almost impossible.

teach.b: Meditations seven, twenty-two, opens, in George Long's translation: "It is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong."
Peculiar here means distinctive, belonging to us: love that doesn't wait for the other person to deserve it. Marcus doesn't just command it.

He gives four reasons that make it possible. They're your kin, part of the same human family. They do wrong through ignorance, without meaning to, the way Socrates taught that nobody does wrong willingly.
Very soon both of you will be dead. And above all, they haven't actually harmed you, because they haven't made your own mind any worse. The second reason is the one people argue with.

Marcus would say they chose it because they misjudged what was good, like someone stumbling in the dark. That's why today's title says stumble. It doesn't excuse the wrong; it changes how you hold the person.
And loving someone who stumbles doesn't mean pretending they didn't, or letting them keep doing it.
Elsewhere in the Meditations, Marcus tells himself to show a wrongdoer the mistake, kindly and without reproach.
The way you'd steady a toddler: firmly, without hatred, and wishing them well.

how: Readers of Marcus sometimes rehearse the four thoughts of 7.22 (kinship, ignorance, mortality, no real harm) when they've been wronged, as a way to wish the person well while still correcting or avoiding the wrong.

s: Marcus says loving wrongdoers is distinctive of human beings
7.22: it is peculiar to man to love even those who do wrong.
Marcus says loving wrongdoers means never correcting them
elsewhere he tells himself to show the wrongdoer the mistake, kindly; the love changes how he holds them, not whether he acts.
the idea that nobody does wrong willingly goes back to Socrates
Marcus draws on it when he says wrongdoers err through ignorance.

games.q: someone lied to you, and you're furious. which thought does Marcus give himself first?
games.why: Meditations 7.22: remember they're kin, they do wrong through ignorance, you'll both soon die, and they haven't harmed your mind.

practice: Bring to mind someone who did you wrong, not the worst thing, just a real one, and try Marcus's four thoughts slowly: they're kin, they stumbled, we'll both be gone soon, they haven't touched who I am.
If you can, wish them well, quietly, in your own words. If you can't today, just sit with the trying.

wordCard.voice: Kin. Marcus's reason to love even wrongdoers: they're part of the same human family, who err without meaning to. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: kin who stumble. Wishing someone well can sit beside firm boundaries. See you tomorrow.
